studies.title: Hepatic mTORC2 activates glycolysis and lipogenesis through Akt, glucokinase, and SREBP1c
studies.finding:
The authors deleted rictor, an essential mTORC2 component, only in mouse liver. In fed knockout mice the liver lost Akt Ser473 phosphorylation and had lower glucokinase and SREBP1c activity, so it kept making glucose (gluconeogenesis) while glycolysis and fat synthesis fell, as if it could not sense that the animal had eaten. The mice became hyperglycaemic and hyperinsulinaemic with low blood lipids. In mTORC2-deficient hepatocytes, constitutively active Akt2 restored both glucose flux and lipogenesis, while extra glucokinase restored glucose flux but not lipogenesis, placing Akt as the main route from hepatic mTORC2 to these outputs.
Boundary: Mouse liver with lifelong genetic loss of mTORC

story: BAS2012 (2012) is BOLERO-2, a phase 3 randomised trial in 724 women with hormone-receptor-positive advanced breast cancer. Adding everolimus to exemestane roughly doubled progression-free survival (10.6 versus 4.1 months by central review). Alejandra Perez is a middle author in the author list. PIC2014 (2014) is the final overall-survival report of BOLERO-2. Median overall survival was 31.0 months with everolimus plus exemestane and 26.6 months with placebo plus exemestane, a difference that was not statistically significant. Alejandra Perez is a middle author in the author list.

PubMed gives no affiliation for this author in the BOLERO-2 primary report. The affiliation here comes from the final overall-survival report, which lists the same author by surname and initials and shares many co-authors with the primary report.

studies.title: Everolimus in postmenopausal hormone-receptor-positive advanced breast cancer (BOLERO-2)
studies.finding: A phase 3 RCT (n=724) proving mTOR matters in a common cancer. Resistance to hormone therapy in breast cancer is associated with mTOR activation. Adding everolimus more than doubled progression-free survival (10.6 vs 4.1 months by central review) - leading to FDA approval. Main toxicity was stomatitis.

studies.title: Everolimus plus exemestane for hormone-receptor-positive, human epidermal growth factor receptor-2-negative advanced breast cancer: overall survival results from BOLERO-2†
studies.finding: This is the final overall-survival report of BOLERO-2, the phase III double-blind trial (published primary analysis: BAS2012) in which postmenopausal women with hormone-receptor-positive, HER2-negative advanced breast cancer that had progressed on a nonsteroidal aromatase inhibitor received exemestane 25 mg/day plus either everolimus 10 mg/day or placebo. Their hearts showed reversal or reduction of several age-related changes in function. RNA sequencing suggested effects on inflammation, metabolism and heart growth. The work is in mice. PubMed lists him at the Buck Institute for Research on Aging.

studies.title: Late-life rapamycin treatment reverses age-related heart dysfunction
studies.finding: Striking evidence that in mice mTOR inhibition doesn't just SLOW aging - it can partly reverse an established age-related phenotype. Giving rapamycin to already-old (24-month) female mice for 3 months improved aged heart function, reversing or attenuating age-related cardiac changes, with RNA-seq changes suggesting anti-hypertrophic and anti-inflammatory effects. Started late, still worked.

current.sub: Buck Institute for Research on Aging (PubMed affiliation, 2015)
story: Remi-Martin Laberge was first author of a 2015 Nature Cell Biology paper in the Atlas (LAB2015), written at the Buck Institute with 20 co-authors. Old, non-dividing (senescent) cells release inflammatory signals called the SASP. The study found that mTOR switches on the production of IL1A, a cytokine near the top of that cascade, and that rapamycin shuts this down. In mice, rapamycin also stopped senescent cells from helping prostate tumours grow.

highlights.LAB2015: First author of the cell and mouse study linking mTOR, IL1A translation and the senescence secretory profile.

pubmed_affiliation: Buck Institute for Research on Aging, Novato, California 94945, USA.

studies.title: mTOR regulates the pro-tumorigenic senescence-associated secretory phenotype by promoting IL1A translation
studies.finding: Explained HOW rapamycin calms 'inflammaging'. Senescent cells spew inflammatory signals (the SASP) that damage surrounding tissue and even feed tumors. mTOR powers this by translating IL1A, the cytokine at the top of the cascade. Rapamycin selectively shuts it down - and blocked senescent cells from fueling prostate tumor growth in mice.

In scar-derived fibroblasts and in a rabbit ear scar model, it lowered collagen and other scar markers, and AKT and mTOR phosphorylation fell at the same time. The authors state that this does not prove the drug works through that pathway.

story: Ashutosh Tiwari was first author of the Atlas study TIW2026 in Genes & Development. It describes a small protein called Firefox (FFX), made from the circular RNA circPVT1. FFX boosts AKT-mTORC1 signalling and cap-dependent translation, which keeps MYC protein levels high. When FFX was removed, MYC levels dropped and tumours grew less in mouse xenograft models of MYC-amplified cancer. PubMed lists Tiwari at the Sanford Burnham Prebys Medical Discovery Institute in La Jolla.

studies.title: Firefox, a protein encoded by circular PVT1, is essential for MYC-driven oncogenesis.
studies.finding: A micropeptide (Firefox/FFX) encoded by the circular RNA circPVT1 stimulates AKT-mTORC1 signaling and cap-dependent translation to sustain MYC protein abundance and transcriptional output. FFX depletion reduces MYC levels and impairs tumor growth in MYC-amplified xenograft models, identifying an mTORC1-linked vulnerability in MYC-driven cancers.

current.sub: Cellular Stress Group, MRC Clinical Sciences Centre, Imperial College, London, UK
story: David Carling is a middle author of a 2011 structural paper on AMPK, the cell's energy sensor that works against mTORC1 when energy is low. The study showed that AMP binding protects AMPK from losing its activating phosphate, that ADP binding at one site gives the same protection without switching the enzyme on, and it reported the crystal structure of an active AMPK complex.

PubMed gives no affiliation for him in this record. The Cellular Stress Group at the MRC Clinical Sciences Centre comes from a 2013 paper by the same team, where PubMed lists him there next to many co-authors of the 2011 study. He is also listed in a second Atlas paper (SEL2009, S6K1 and lifespan in mice), but that study is not covered here because the available records did not confirm the same affiliation.

highlights.XIA2011: Middle author of the paper on the structure of mammalian AMPK and its regulation by ADP.

pubmed_affiliation: MRC Clinical Sciences Centre, Cellular Stress Group, Hammersmith Hospital Campus, Imperial College, DuCane Road, London W12 0NN, UK.

studies.title: Structure of mammalian AMPK and its regulation by ADP
studies.finding: AMP binding to the gamma regulatory domain promotes phosphorylation of AMPK and protects it from dephosphorylation. ADP binding to one site also protects against dephosphorylation but does not activate allosterically. Crystal structure of an active AMPK complex.

pubmed_affiliation: Center for Cardiovascular and Muscular Diseases, Sanford Burnham Prebys Medical Discovery Institute, San Diego, CA, USA

studies.title: Strengthening Muscle for Healthy Ageing: Innovative Treatments for Sarcopenia
studies.finding: A major pharma-facing review (Blau lab, Stanford/Sanford Burnham) surveying emerging drug strategies for sarcopenia — the age-related loss of muscle mass/strength with no approved therapy. Among the pleiotropic mechanisms discussed, mTORC1 inhibitors are highlighted specifically for their ability to restore impaired autophagy in aging muscle, alongside NAD-related molecules, urolithin A, myostatin inhibitors, SARMs, and 15-PGDH ('gerozyme') inhibitors. Useful high-level context for where mTORC1 modulation sits among competing anti-sarcopenia strategies, though it does not itself address dynamic/temporal mTOR activity.
